hub.description: Decks and fences in Eagleville, TN, planned for rural lots where limestone, rolling ground, septic fields, and long runs across acreage shape the job.
hub.intro: Eagleville is a small town in the southwest corner of Rutherford County, and many of the properties around it sit on several acres. That changes how you plan a deck or a fence. On an Eagleville lot, a deck might face open pasture instead of the house next door. Fences often have to cover a long stretch of ground and still hold a dog. This page walks through the questions people in Eagleville tend to ask first, and points you to our deck and fence pages for more detail.

sections.heading: What a bigger lot changes
paragraphs: The biggest difference between many Eagleville properties and a town lot is room, and room gives you choices a subdivision lot does not. A deck can go where the evening shade falls, not just where the back door happens to be. You can fence the yard around the house and leave the fields open. The trade is distance. Materials may have to come down a long gravel drive, and a fence line that looks short from the porch often runs much longer once you walk it with a measuring wheel.

Whether your place sits close to Downtown Eagleville or out on a farm near Allisona, walk the property and decide what the deck or fence actually needs to do. Keeping a dog close to the house is a different job from keeping cattle off the road. A deck built for summer cookouts needs different things than one meant for quiet mornings looking out at the field. Knowing the job keeps the estimate focused and keeps you from paying for fence you did not need.

sections.heading: Decks for Eagleville homes
paragraphs: Homes around Eagleville range from older farmhouses to newer builds, and each brings its own deck questions. An older house may need its rim board checked before a deck is fastened to it, or the deck may stand on its own posts instead. A newer house on a sloped lot often has a back door set high off the ground, which means taller posts and a longer set of stairs. Open lots with few big trees get a lot of afternoon sun, so the decking you pick matters. Our [Eagleville deck builder page](/deck-builder-eagleville-tn/) covers footings and materials in more depth.

sections.heading: Fences for country property
paragraphs: Fence work around Eagleville often goes past a small backyard square. Many owners want a yard fence that keeps the dog near the house, and some also need a longer line along the road or around a pasture. Gates need more thought out here, since a pasture gate may have to open wide enough for a tractor or a trailer. Animals change the design too. A fence that keeps a Labrador in the yard may not stop a goat. The [Eagleville fence company page](/fence-company-eagleville-tn/) goes deeper into gates and property lines.

sections.heading: Rock and rolling ground
paragraphs: Much of Rutherford County sits on limestone, and it is common to hit rock when digging post holes or footings around Eagleville. In some spots it is a loose layer that breaks apart. Elsewhere it is solid ledge that takes a rock bit and extra time. Nobody can promise what is under a given spot until the hole is dug, so a fair estimate explains how rock would be handled. Many lots here also roll, so fence panels may need to step down a hill and a deck may sit low at one end and high at the other. Our guide on [fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) explains the choices.

sections.heading: Permits, HOAs, and buried lines
paragraphs: Some Eagleville homes sit inside the town limits, and many others with an Eagleville mailing address sit out in unincorporated Rutherford County. Which office reviews a deck or a fence can depend on which side of that line you are on, and the rules are not the same everywhere. Check with the town or the county codes office before you build. If your home is in a newer subdivision, read your HOA covenants too, since many require approval before a fence or deck goes up. Call Tennessee 811 before any digging so public utility lines get marked.

sections.heading: What to have ready for an estimate
paragraphs: A few details make an Eagleville estimate more useful. It helps to know roughly where your septic tank and drain field are, since neither a deck nor fence posts should go on top of them. If the fence follows a property line, have a plat or survey handy. Think about what needs to pass through each gate and what animals the fence has to hold. Photos of the spot help too. When you are ready, [request an estimate](#estimate) and tell us what you are planning.

faqs.q: Should we build the deck or the fence first?
faqs.a: Usually the deck goes first, especially on a big Eagleville lot where equipment or a load of lumber needs a clear path to the back of the house. Once a fence is up, that path may be blocked or limited to a single gate. If you need a fence right away for a dog, put a gate wide enough for equipment in the spot where the deck work will need to come through.

faqs.q: Do I have to fence my whole property in Eagleville?
faqs.a: No. Plenty of owners fence only the yard around the house and leave the rest open, or add a pasture line later. Fence is usually priced by the foot, so the length of the run is one of the biggest factors in the cost. On acreage that adds up fast. Start with the job the fence has to do and fence that area first. You can extend it later.

faqs.q: Will rock in the ground raise the price of an Eagleville project?
faqs.a: It can. Rock slows digging and sometimes calls for a rock bit or a change in footing plans, and around Eagleville that happens often enough to plan for. The honest answer is that no one knows exactly until the holes are dug. A good estimate should explain how rock would be handled and whether it changes the price, so you are not surprised halfway through the job.

deck.description: Deck builder for Eagleville, TN homes. Decks planned around shallow rock, rolling ground, septic fields, and full sun on rural lots and newer yards.
deck.intro: If you are looking for a deck builder in Eagleville, your lot probably gives you more room to work with than most. That is good news, but it brings questions town lots do not, like where a deck should sit when the whole back of the house faces open ground, and what happens when a footing hole hits rock close to the septic field. This page answers the deck questions that come up most on rural lots around Eagleville, whether your house is an older farmhouse or a newer build near Downtown Eagleville.

sections.heading: Choosing a spot for a deck on an Eagleville lot
paragraphs: On a small lot the deck goes off the back door and that is the end of it. Out here you often have options. Think about when you will use it. A deck on the west side takes the full heat of a summer afternoon, and many cleared lots have no big trees near the house to soften it. An east or north exposure stays cooler in the evening. If the best view is a pasture or a tree line, it may be worth angling the deck or setting it off the side of the house to face that way.

Wind is easy to overlook. Open fields let a breeze build across the property, and that breeze pushes on umbrellas and shade structures. If you plan a pergola or a roof over part of the deck, tell your Eagleville deck builder early so the posts and footings can be sized for it from the start rather than added later.

sections.heading: Footings when you hit Rutherford County rock
paragraphs: Limestone sits close to the surface across much of Rutherford County, and many Eagleville lots have it only a short way down. A footing hole that starts in clay can stop hard on rock well before it reaches the depth the plan calls for. When that happens there are a few ways to handle it. Sometimes a rock bit gets through. Other times the footing shifts a short distance to softer ground, and some codes offices will allow a footing that bears directly on solid rock. The inspector for your address has the final word, so the footing plan should be settled with them before the concrete goes in.

sections.heading: Septic fields, wells, and buried lines
paragraphs: Many homes around Eagleville rely on a septic system rather than a sewer line, so the first question on a rural lot is where the tank and drain field sit. A deck should not go on top of either one. Footings can crack pipes and the weight can compact the drain field. The tank lid also needs to stay reachable for pumping. If you are not sure where yours is, the original septic permit or a septic service company can often help you find it.

Wells and private lines matter too. Tennessee 811 notifies the utilities so they can mark their own lines, but that usually does not cover lines you own, such as a water line to a barn or a power line run out to a shop. Before any footings go in, point out everything you know is buried, and keep the well head clear of the deck footprint so it can still be serviced.

sections.heading: Farmhouses and newer builds in Eagleville
paragraphs: Older farmhouses around Eagleville can be a good fit for a deck, but they deserve a careful look first. The band board where a deck would attach may be soft with age or framed in a way that does not match modern connections. When that is the case, a freestanding deck on its own posts, set just off the house, is often the safer choice. It also avoids opening up old siding and trim to bolt a ledger in place.

Newer homes bring different questions. On a sloped lot the back door may sit high off the yard, so a deck needs tall posts with good bracing and a long run of stairs. The soil around new construction is often disturbed fill, which can keep settling for a few seasons. Footings need to reach firm ground below it, and the yard grade should carry rainwater away from the posts instead of toward them.

sections.heading: Deck boards that can take open sun
paragraphs: Pressure treated pine is one of the most common deck materials in Middle Tennessee, and it holds up well when it is sealed and kept clean. In full sun it tends to check and gray faster, so plan on regular upkeep. Composite boards skip the staining but can get hot underfoot on a bright afternoon, especially darker colors on a deck with no shade. If your Eagleville deck will face west across an open yard, set a sample board in the sun and touch it at midday before you choose. Our comparison of [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) goes through the tradeoffs.

Railings deserve the same thought on an open lot. Wide wood balusters block more of the view than people expect once they sit down. Thin metal balusters or cable keep the sightline to the field clearer, though they usually cost more and have their own upkeep. If you can, look at a finished railing of each type in person before you decide.

sections.heading: Getting materials to the back of the property
paragraphs: Access is a real question on rural Eagleville lots. Lumber and concrete may need to travel across a yard or pasture to reach the build site, and wet ground after a few days of rain can turn a truck path into ruts. Point out soft spots and low places that hold water, and mark where the septic field is so no one drives over it. On some properties it makes sense to wait for the ground to firm up. If a fence is part of your plans too, build the deck first or leave a wide gate, and see our [Eagleville fence page](/fence-company-eagleville-tn/) for gate planning.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Eagleville?
faqs.a: In most places, attached decks and raised decks need a permit, and some low decks do too. The office that handles it depends on whether your home is inside Eagleville town limits or out in Rutherford County, and the rules differ. Call the right codes office before work starts, and check your HOA covenants if you have them. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains how the process usually works.

faqs.q: Can a deck be built away from the house?
faqs.a: Yes. A freestanding deck sits on its own posts and footings and does not attach to the house at all. On a big Eagleville lot that opens up options, like a deck out by a pond or under a big shade tree. It still needs solid footings, and a permit may still apply, so check before you plan it. You will also want a path to it that stays dry after rain.

faqs.q: How should I compare quotes from deck builders?
faqs.a: Line the quotes up item by item. Check that each one covers the same size and height and uses the same decking and railing. Then ask how each builder handles rock. One may assume clean digging and adjust later, while another prices some rock work in from the start. Also ask whether the permit and removal of an old deck are included. Two numbers only mean something once the scope matches.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before asking a deck builder for a price?
faqs.a: A rough idea of size and where the deck should go is enough to start. Photos of the back of the house help, along with a note on how high the door sits off the ground. On a rural lot, know where the septic tank and drain field are, and mention any buried lines to a barn or shop. If your home is in a subdivision, have your HOA rules handy.

faqs.q: Can a new deck tie into the old porch on my farmhouse?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Many older porches sit on piers, and some have been patched more than once over the years. Joining a new deck to it only works if that framing is sound and the heights line up. If the porch is out of level or the piers have shifted, it is often better to build the deck as its own structure beside the porch and connect the two with a step.

fence.description: Fence installation in Eagleville, TN on rural lots: how much land to fence, gate width, animals, rock in post holes, and old lines that miss the deed.
fence.intro: Fence installation around Eagleville usually starts with a simple question: what does this fence need to keep in, and what does it need to block from view? On a smaller lot near Downtown Eagleville the answer is often a privacy fence around the backyard. Out on acreage toward Allisona it might be that plus a longer line along the road, with a gate wide enough for a tractor. This page covers what Eagleville owners should think through before they call a fence company, from rock in the post holes to where the property line really is.

sections.heading: How much of your Eagleville land to fence
paragraphs: Fences are usually priced by the linear foot, so on a big lot the length of the run tends to be the biggest factor in the cost. Walk the line before you ask for a price. Many Eagleville owners find that a fenced yard around the house handles the everyday job of keeping a dog close and giving kids room to play. The rest of the land can stay open or get a simpler farm fence later. Our guide on [what drives fence cost in Middle Tennessee](/guides/fence-cost-middle-tennessee/) explains the other things that move the number.

It also helps to decide early what style belongs where. A privacy fence near the house and a lower, more open fence farther out can look fine together if the posts and colors are planned as one job. Putting them up years apart without a plan is how a property ends up with fence styles that do not match.

sections.heading: Privacy fence close to the house
paragraphs: A privacy fence on a rural Eagleville lot usually has a specific job, like screening a busy road or blocking the view of a neighbor's shop. Board on board and shadowbox styles are common choices because they block the view well from straight on. On open ground, a solid fence also catches a lot of wind. That puts more load on the posts, so post depth and spacing tend to matter more here than in a sheltered subdivision yard. Ask how the posts will be set and how far apart they will be before you sign anything.

sections.heading: Gates wide enough for what you drive through
paragraphs: On country property around Eagleville, gates are often where a fence plan goes wrong. Walk gates are simple. A gate for a tractor with a bush hog, or for a truck pulling a trailer, needs more planning. Measure the widest thing that will ever pass through and leave room to spare, since a trailer rarely lines up perfectly. Wide gates are heavy, so the posts that hold them need to be set deeper and braced well, or the gate can start to sag. Double gates that meet in the middle can help on long spans.

Placement matters as much as width. Put equipment gates where the ground is fairly level and where you can pull straight in. A gate on a slope may drag on the uphill side when it swings. Think about which way it opens too, especially if animals will be crowding the gate at feeding time.

sections.heading: Fencing around animals in Eagleville
paragraphs: The right fence depends on what it holds. Dogs are one of the most common reasons people fence a yard, and the usual worries are jumping and digging. A solid privacy fence helps with a dog that barks at every truck on the road, while a dog that digs needs the gap at the bottom closed or a barrier along the base. Our guide to [the best fence for dogs](/guides/best-fence-for-dogs/) covers the details.

Livestock is a different job. Many horses chew wood and lean on fences, and they do best with a fence they can see clearly. Goats often climb and squeeze through gaps that would hold a calf. A fence designed only for privacy may not be the right design for livestock, so if animals will share the fenced area, tell the fence company what they are before anyone draws a plan. On Eagleville acreage, that question comes up more than it does in town.

sections.heading: Rock, slope, and old fence lines
paragraphs: Post holes around Eagleville often hit limestone, sometimes close to the surface and sometimes farther down. When the auger stops, a rock bit can usually finish the hole, or the post can shift a little to find softer ground. Rolling ground adds another layer. Panels either step down the hill in level sections or rack to follow the slope, and each approach leaves a different gap at the bottom that matters if you have a small dog.

Many rural lots also have an old fence along the boundary, often rusted wire with trees grown into it. Taking it out is extra work, and sometimes the old line is not where the property line actually is. Decide before the estimate whether the old fence comes out or stays where it is while the new line goes in beside it.

sections.heading: Property lines and rules around Eagleville
paragraphs: Old farm fences and tree lines do not always follow the deed. Before a new fence goes up on a boundary, find the property pins or get a survey, and talk with the neighbor on that side. Contact Tennessee 811 so buried utilities get marked, and keep in mind that a water line you ran to a well house or barn is yours to locate. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) goes into more detail.

Rules for fence height and placement near a road can differ between land within the town and unincorporated county land, so confirm with the right codes office before you build. Newer subdivisions may also have HOA covenants that set fence style and color. A few calls up front cost far less than moving a finished fence.

faqs.q: Can a fence company tell me where my property line is?
faqs.a: Not with any authority. A fence company can find pins you already have and follow a line you show them, but only a surveyor can mark the boundary. Older deeds in rural Tennessee sometimes describe lines by landmarks that are long gone, which makes a survey worth the cost when an Eagleville fence runs close to the edge. If the fence sits well inside your line, you may not need one.

faqs.q: Will rock in the ground stop my fence installation?
faqs.a: It usually slows the work rather than stopping it. Around Eagleville, many post holes hit limestone somewhere along a long run. A rock bit or a small shift in post spacing handles most of it, though it takes extra time. What rock does change is labor, so ask how each estimate treats it. A bid that assumes easy digging everywhere may not be the final number.

faqs.q: Which side of the fence should face out?
faqs.a: Many HOAs and some local rules expect the finished side to face the neighbor or the road. On a rural Eagleville lot with no rule on the matter and no neighbor close by, the choice is yours. Some owners pick a shadowbox or board on board style so both sides look finished and the question goes away. Check your covenants first if you live in a subdivision.

faqs.q: Should old barbed wire come out before a new fence goes in?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the new fence follows the same line. Many older farms around Eagleville still have wire along the boundary. Old wire gets in the way of post holes and can wrap around equipment, and it is a hazard for horses. If the old fence sits on a line you are not sure about, leave it alone until the boundary is confirmed, since it may be one of the only markers you have.

faqs.q: Do I need HOA approval for a fence in Eagleville?
faqs.a: Only if your home is in a subdivision with covenants, and many rural parcels around Eagleville have none. If you do have an HOA, expect the review board to want a drawing of the fence line and a description of the style before you build. Approval can take a while, so plan your timing around it. Our guide to [getting HOA approval](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) walks through a clean submission.
